newsitem.title: USA: Continental pilots open talks on new pact.
newsitem.headline: Continental pilots open talks on new pact.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc.'s pilots union said Wednesday it is seeking wage increases that would bring its members up to par with salaries paid to pilots of other large U.S. carriers.

In a proposed labour pact presented to the company Wednesday, the Independent Association of Continental Pilots also sought improvements in their retirement plan, a steep increase in vacation days and an overhaul of the airline's scheduling system.

"By the close of these negotiations, our pilots must have industry-standard compensation; that is, pay and benefits comparable to those earned by pilots at the other leading carriers," union President Len Nikolai said in a letter to Continental Chairman Gordon Bethune.

The union, which represents 4,000 Continental pilots, said it was optimistic about completing talks on a new labour pact before the current contract expires on June 30. The union also will hold talks on a new pact for 1,000 Continental Express pilots whose contract expires Oct. 1, Nikolai said.
"We were encouraged by your agreement to a simultaneous signing date for both the Continental and Continental Express contracts," Nikolai said.
Bethune conferred with union negotiators at a breakfast meeting Wednesday and reiterated an earlier pledge to improve the pilots' pay and benefits, Nikolai said in the letter.

Bethune, who is widely credited with boosting morale of the airlines' workers, also said he would ensure a fair seniority system was in place for the Continental pilots in the event of a merger, Nikolai said.

The union said Continental pilots averaged $92,000 a year in taxable wages, well below the $150,000 paid to pilots at United Airlines, the nation's largest carrier, and the $130,000 paid to US Airways Group Inc. pilots.
Pilots at Continental, the nation's fifth-largest airline, also receive 21 annual vacation days, well below an industry standard 44 days for pilots, the union said.
The union also is seeking an overhaul of a system that requires Continental pilots to be available in "sitting reserve" without being paid.
Union negotiators said there was no dispute over Continental's use of regional 50-seat jets, an issue that caused considerable turbulence in American Airlines' talks with its pilots.
"Unlike the pilots at American Airlines we do not propose to interfere with the company's ability to utilize 50-seat regional jets under the Continental Express certificate," Nikolai said.
Continental Express pilots are seeking a raise from an average $13,000 annual starting salary and a pension plan, scheduling changes and security in the event of a merger.

Separately, Spain's Iberia, which own 10 percent of Aerolineas Argentinas, said American and Continental were interested in buying a stake in the Argentinian carrier and could own a 20 percent share in the next two months.

Iberia sources said, however, that the Spanish airline would not sell its own stake. Continental or American may buy the stake from Aerolineas' major shareholder Andes Holdings, which currently holds a 63 percent stake.
"We should know in the next 10 to 15 days which airline has succeeded in securing the stake," said one source.
Continental's class A stock fell 12.5 cents to $30.875 on the New York Stock Exchange in early afternoon trading.
